¶
'''tomfool''' (tom′föl′), ''v. i.'' [< ''tomfool'', ''n.''] To act foolishly and triflingly. [Colloq.]

{{smaller block|“And leave you to go ''tomfooling'' out there again?” asks Jim.
{{right|''Rhoda Broughton'', Alas, xxix.}}}}

'''tomfoolery''' (tom′fö′lėr-i), ''n.'' [< ''tomfool'' + ''-er-y''.] 1. Foolish trifling; ridiculous behavior; nonsense.

{{smaller block|“Foolery” was thought of old sufficiently expressive; nothing short of ''tomfoolery'' will do now.
{{right|''Landor'', Imag. Conv., Archdeacon Hare and W. Landor.}}}}

2. Silly trifles; absurd ornaments or knickknacks.

{{smaller block|The bride must have a trousseau of laces, satins, jewel-boxes, and ''tomfoolery''.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Book of Snobs, xxxvi.}}}}

'''tomfoolish''' (tom′fö′lish), ''a.'' [< ''tomfool'' + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.] Like a tomfool; apt to indulge in tomfoolery. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|A man he is by nature merry,
Somewhat ''Tom-foolish'', and comical, very.
{{right|''Southey'', Nondescripts, viii. (''Davies.'')}}}}

¶
'''tomjohn''' (tom′jon), ''n.'' Same as ''tonjon.''

'''tomkin-post''' (tom′kin-pōst), ''n.'' In a grain-mill, the post supporting the pivot-end of the bridge-tree. ''E. H. Knight.''

'''tomling''' (tom′ling), ''n.'' [< ''tom''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ling.''] A male kitten. ''Southey,'' Letters. (''Davies.'') [Rare.]

'''tomly†''', ''adv.'' A Middle English form of ''toomly.''

'''tommy''' (tom′i), ''n.''; pl. ''tommies'' (-iz). [Perhaps a particular application of ''Tommy,'' a familiar dim. of ''Tom:'' see ''tom''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' Originally, a penny roll; hence, bread; provisions; especially, goods given to a workman in lieu of wages. [In this and the next two uses slang, Eng.]

{{smaller block|The employers . . . supplied them [the miners] with food in order that they might spend no money save in the truck-shops or ''tommy-shops.''
{{right|''Hinton'', Eng. Radical Leaders, p. 145.}}}}

'''tom-noddy''' (tom′nod′i), ''n.'' [Also, corruptly, ''tom-norry''; < ''tom''<sup>1</sup> + ''noddy''<sup>1</sup>.] 1. The puffin or sea-parrot. Also ''tommy-noddy'', and ''tom-norry'' or ''tammy-norie.'' See cut under ''puffin.'' [Prov. Eng.]—2. A blockhead; a dolt; a dunce; a fool.

'''tom-norry''' (tom′nor′i), ''n.'' [Also ''tammy-norie'': see ''tom-noddy.''] Same as ''tom-noddy'', 1. [Scotch.]

'''tom-noup''' (tom′nöp), ''n.'' [< ''tom''<sup>1</sup> + ''noup'', var. of ''nope.''] The black-headed tomtit, or greater titmouse, ''Parus major.'' See cut under ''Parus.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''Tomobranchia''' (tō-mọ̄-brang′ki-ä̤), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < Gr. τομός, cut (< τέμνειν, ταμεῖν, cut), + βράγχια, gills: see ''branchiæ.''] In J. E. Gray's classification (1821), one of three orders of ''Saccophora'', or ascidians, distinguished from ''Holobranchia'' and from ''Diphyllobranchia.''

'''to-morn†''', ''adv.'' [ME. ''to morwen, to morgen, to margen'', etc.: see ''to-morrow'', and cf. ''morn, morrow.''] To-morrow. ''Chaucer.''

'''to-morrow, tomorrow''' (tọ̈-mor′ō), ''adv.'' and ''n.'' [< ME. ''to morwe, to morȝe'', also ''to morwen, to morȝen'' (see ''to-morn''), < AS. ''tō morgen, tō mergen, tō merigen'', on the morrow, in the morning: ''tō'', to, on; ''morgen, mergen, merigen'', dat. of ''morgen'', morrow: see ''morrow, morn.'' Cf. ''to-day, to-night.''] '''I.''' ''adv.'' On the morrow; on the day after the present.

{{smaller block|That Mede ys thus ymaryed ''to-morwe'' thow shalt aspie.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), iii. 46.}}}}

'''Tom-poker''' (tom′pō′kėr), ''n.'' [< ''Tom''<sup>1</sup> + ''poker''<sup>2</sup>.] A bugbear to frighten children. [Prov. Eng.]

'''tompon''' (tom′pon), ''n.'' Same as ''tompion''<sup>1</sup>, 2.

'''tom-pudding''' (tom′pud′ing), ''n.'' [< ''tom''<sup>1</sup> + ''pudding''.] The little grebe, or dabchick. [Prov. Eng. and Irish.]

'''tomrig†''' (tom′rig), ''n.'' [< ''tom''<sup>1</sup> + ''rig''<sup>3</sup>.] A rude, wild girl; a tomboy.

{{smaller block|The author represents Belinda a fine, modest, well-bred lady, and yet in the very next canto she appears an arrant ramp and ''tomrig''.
{{right|''Dennis'', On Pope's Rape of the Lock, p. 16. (''Latham.'')}}}}

'''tomtit''' (tom′tit′), ''n.'' [< ''tom''<sup>1</sup> + ''tit''<sup>2</sup>.] Some little bird; a tit or titling. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') A titmouse of any kind. See ''Parinæ''. (''b'') The tree-creeper, ''Certhia familiaris''. [Irish.] (''c'') The wren, ''Troglodytes parvulus''. [Local, Eng.] (''d'') The green tody of Jamaica, ''Todus viridis''. See cut under ''tody''. readings.c3s2:
1. In India, the drum used by musicians, jugglers, public criers, etc.—2. Same as ''gong''<sup>2</sup>, 1.

'''tom-tom''' (tom′tom), ''v. i.'' [< ''tom-tom'', ''n.''] To beat on a tom-tom. ''Sala'', Trip to Barbary, 1866.

'''tom-trot''' (tom′trot′), ''n.'' A sweetmeat for children, made by melting sugar, butter, and treacle together. When it is cooling and rather stiff, it is drawn out into pieces. ''Halliwell.''

{{smaller block|I want toffy; I have been eating ''Tom Trot'' all day.
{{right|''Disraeli'', Coningsby, i. 9.}}}}

'''tom-turkey''' (tom′tėr″ki), ''n.'' [< ''tom''<sup>1</sup> + ''turkey.''] A turkey-cock.

{{smaller block|I never heard that a ''tom-turkey'' would set on eggs.
{{right|''H. B. Stowe'', Oldtown, p. 64.}}}}

'''ton<sup>1</sup>''' (tun), ''n.'' [A form of ''tun'', phonetically archaic, retained in designations of measure prob. by reason of its use in statutes, where the F. and ML. forms are usually favored: see ''tun''<sup>1</sup>.] 1†. A cask; hence, a measure of capacity used for wine. See ''tun''<sup>1</sup>, 1.—2. A measure of capacity: used (''a'') for timber, 40 feet of oak or ash timber, sometimes 48 or 50 feet of hewn; (''b'') for flour, 8 sacks or 10 barrels; (''c'') for potatoes, 10 to 36 bushels; (''d'') for wheat, 20 bushels; (''e'') for earth or gravel, 1 cubic yard, sometimes 23 cubic feet; (''f'') for grindstones, 15 cubic feet; (''g'') for Portland stone, 16 cubic feet; (''h'') for salt, 42 bushels; (''i'') for lime, 40 bushels; (''j'') for coke, 28 bushels; (''k'') for the carrying capacity of a ship, 40 cubic feet (this is what is called the ''actual tonnage:'' see ''tonnage'').

{{smaller block|Here arrived yesterday a Dutch ship of 300 ''tons'', with 250 ''tons'' of salt, sent by Mr. Onge from Lisbon.
{{right|''Winthrop'', Hist. New England, II. 430.}}}}
